content.chapter: Chapter 1: Al-Andalus and Its Place in Spain
objectives: Summarize the time span and place of Muslim rule in Al-Andalus.
Explain why the 781-year presence is remarkable, using the although-clause.
Identify the cities and the present-day status of the region.
Use non-defining which-clauses, as well as and had ever + past participle.
content.pedagogy: A short, dense opening chapter. Its long sentences pack several facts each, so the lesson unpacks them: one fact per line on the board, then the learners rebuild the sentence. This prepares them for the clause structures of the whole book.
priorKnowledge: Relative clauses with which and who.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The territory shrank, but the presence lasted; the although-clause does not mean the lands grew.
Andalusia today is a region of Spain, not a separate country.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: although + clause · non-defining which-clause · as well as · superlative + had ever + past participle · were known as
Notice (Activity 1): what the although-clause does.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose which / as well as / had ever, then reformulate with despite + -ing, never … such a(n) and an active verb.
Likely errors: *, that includes … · *as well in other fields · *the West has ever seen (about a past period).
Use (Activity 4): a region and its heritage.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: i-BE-ri-an pe-NIN-su-la, an-da-LU-si-a, GRA-na-da, COR-do-ba, se-VIL-ya.
Stress: ter-ri-TO-ry /ˈterətɔːri/, in-VAL-u-a-ble, au-TON-o-mous.
beforeReading: Show a map of the Iberian Peninsula. Ask: “Which two countries are here today? Which cities do you know?”
duringReading: First reading: find the two dates and the number of years.
Unpack the although-sentence into two facts.
Second reading: find the fields in which invaluable works were produced.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook; 5–12 First reading and dates; 12–18 Unpacking long sentences; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a region and its heritage; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is a 781-year presence remarkable if the territory shrank?
Which fields does the chapter name?
What does “autonomous community” tell us about Spain today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “781 Years” and “Andalusia Today” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: territory, shrank, steadily, numerous, invaluable, autonomous.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two facts of the although-sentence on separate cards to join.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a two-sentence summary of the chapter with although and as well as.

formativeAssessment: States the dates and the 781 years.
Explains the contrast in the although-sentence.
Uses which, as well as and had ever correctly.
expectedResponses: Muslims ruled much of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492. Although their territory shrank after the 11th century, their presence lasted 781 years, and they produced invaluable works in art and architecture as well as medicine, literature and philosophy.
content.transferTask: Describe a region whose past still shapes its present.
content.teacherReflection: Did unpacking the long sentences help learners read the rest of the book?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with although and one with a non-defining which-clause about Al-Andalus.

rubricLevels.secure: States the time span and the region.
Uses which, as well as and had ever.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Beginning of Muslim Spain
objectives: Describe the start of the conquest in 711 and its speed.
Analyze the strengths of the conquerors and the weaknesses of the Visigothic Kingdom.
Distinguish reported facts from attributed views.
Use reduced participle clauses, It is known that and As … say.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains a historical event through its causes. A two-sided cause chart (conquerors / Visigothic Kingdom) shows that the speed of the conquest was not only military. The chapter also models academic reporting: It is known that … and As some historians say …
priorKnowledge: The words army, governor and conquest.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The army was mostly Berber, not mostly Arab.
The text says some cities opened their gates, not all of them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reduced participle clauses (driven by, made up of, caused by) · It is known that … · As some historians say, … · have a hard time + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): driven by = who were driven by.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose reporting forms, then reduce three relative clauses.
Likely errors: *It knows that · *Like some historians say · *a hard time to deal.
Use (Activity 4): explaining a fast change.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: TÂ-rık b. zi-YÂD, MÛ-sâ b. nu-SAYR, TAN-gier, to-LE-do, i-FRI-qi-ya, VIS-i-goths.
Stress: con-QUEST, de-TER-mined, dis-SAT-is-fied, SAV-iors.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can make a country easy to conquer? Think of problems inside the country.”
duringReading: First reading: complete a time line for 711–714.
Second reading: fill the two-sided cause chart.
Find the sentence that gives a historian’s view.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–13 First reading and time line; 13–20 Cause chart; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: explaining a fast change; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did most people view the Muslims as saviors?
Which Visigothic policy affected the Jews?
Is “grave internal weaknesses” a fact or a view? How do we know?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Tangier to Toledo” and “Three Years” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: dates back to, determined, conquest, made up, captured, roughly, dealing with, internal conflicts, unrest, dissatisfied with, saviors, grave.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the cause chart with the headings and one example on each side.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph: “Why was the conquest so fast?” with two causes from each side.

formativeAssessment: Separates fact (It is known that) from view (As some historians say).
Uses a reduced participle clause correctly.
expectedResponses: The conquest was fast because the conquerors were determined soldiers driven by a strong belief, while the Visigothic Kingdom was weakened by internal conflicts, social unrest and the policy of forcing Jews to become Christians.
content.transferTask: Explain why a change in your community happened quickly.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners distinguish the facts from the historians’ view?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with a participle clause and one with “It is known that” about the conquest.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: A Golden Age of Culture
objectives: Describe the cultural level of Al-Andalus with evidence (cities, numbers, thinkers).
Explain what set the civilization apart.
Compare the urban Islamic bloc and the agricultural Christian bloc.
Use inversion after not only, comparatives and “stand out against”.
content.pedagogy: A rich descriptive chapter. Learners collect evidence (thinkers, numbers, cities) in a table and then compare two systems with a Venn diagram. The inversion “not only did …” is the key B2 structure of the book; it is noticed here and recycled later.
priorKnowledge: The words urban, rural and trade.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Medieval Christians” were impressed by Al-Andalus; the text does not say they lived in Al-Andalus.
The two blocs came into contact; they did not become one system.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not only + auxiliary + subject (inversion) · comparative / superlative · stand out against · set something apart
Notice (Activity 1): inversion after not only.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose comparative forms, then rewrite with inversion and sets apart.
Likely errors: *Not only different cultures came · *more high · *stood out from the barrenness (meaning shift).
Use (Activity 4): what makes a golden age?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ibn al-A-ra-bi, ibn RUSHD, ibn tu-FAYL, va-LEN-ci-a.
Stress: re-NOWNED, CON-tem-po-rar-y /kənˈtempəreri/, so-ci-o-e-co-NOM-ic, ag-ri-CUL-tur-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “What would you expect to find in a very advanced medieval city?” List ideas.
duringReading: First reading: complete an evidence table (thinkers / numbers / cities).
Second reading: Venn diagram of the two blocs.
Find what happened to the Mediterranean.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–14 First reading and evidence table; 14–20 Venn diagram; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: what makes a golden age?; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What evidence shows that Al-Andalus was in a golden age?
What set its civilization apart from other Islamic regions?
Why was the change of the Mediterranean important?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Thinkers of the Age” and “The Roman Lake” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: renowned, possessed, impressed, pointed out, barrenness, contemporary, sets it apart, distinct, came into contact, conducted, operated, agricultural, dominated.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the evidence table with the headings and the paragraph numbers.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph comparing the two blocs with whereas and not only … but also.

expectedResponses: Not only did different cultures come together in Al-Andalus, but two distinct systems also came into contact: the urban Islamic bloc with a monetary economy and the agricultural Christian bloc dominated by rural life.
content.transferTask: Define a golden age and support it with evidence.
content.teacherReflection: Did the evidence table help learners avoid general praise?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “Not only did …, but … also …” about this chapter.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Umayyad State in Al-Andalus
objectives: Explain why the advance into the Iberian Peninsula seemed natural.
Trace the Umayyad period from 756 to 1031 on a time line.
Describe the groups of the population and the effort to maintain harmony.
Use it seems natural that … would, the past perfect and was characterized by.
content.pedagogy: A chapter of dates and groups. A time line with two colours (before 756 / 756–1031) shows how the past perfect works, and a population web shows the groups. The key idea is the effort to build a culture of living together.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Umayyads in Al-Andalus continued a family that had ruled in the East; they were not a new family.
New converts “later outnumbered” the Arab Muslims; this was not true from the start.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It seems natural that … would + verb · past perfect active and passive (had conquered, had been driven) · was characterized by
Notice (Activity 1): would as an expected past result.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the tenses, then sort the facts on a time line.
Likely errors: *who conquered … by 710 (missing earlier past) · *had driven (active instead of passive) · *the era characterized by (missing was).
Use (Activity 4): a period characterized by …
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: um-AY-yads, ab-BA-sids, abd al-rah-MAN.
Stress: MAIN-tain /meɪnˈteɪn/, CHAR-ac-ter-ized, out-NUM-bered.
beforeReading: Ask: “If an army has conquered all of North Africa, where might it go next? Look at the map.”
duringReading: First reading: complete the time line (710, 750, 756, 1031).
Second reading: list the groups of the population.
Find how many times the throne changed hands.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook; 5–13 First reading and time line; 13–19 Population web; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a period characterized by …; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the advance into the peninsula seem natural?
What does “changed hands 19 times” suggest about the period?
Why did the rulers try to maintain harmony?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “From Damascus to Córdoba” and “Many Peoples” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: advance, changed hands, maintain.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the dates and the first word of each event.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph about the Umayyad period with had been, was characterized by and outnumbered.

formativeAssessment: Places the events on the time line correctly.
Names the groups of the population.
expectedResponses: The Umayyads, who had been driven from power by the Abbasids in 750, gained new power in Al-Andalus in 756. The period until 1031 was characterized by rulers’ efforts to maintain harmony among Arabs, Berbers, new converts, Slavs, Christians and Jews.
content.transferTask: Describe what a period in your school or town was characterized by.
content.teacherReflection: Did the two-colour time line make the past perfect clear?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “had been” and one with “was characterized by” about this chapter.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the groups of the population.
Uses the past perfect and was characterized by.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: Abd al-Rahman III and the Caliphate
objectives: Explain how Abd al-Rahman III restored the prestige of the state at home and abroad.
Explain why he declared himself caliph and why he issued gold coins.
Analyze his policy towards the Arab nobility and the other groups.
Use on the condition that, partly due to, whose and by + -ing.
content.pedagogy: A chapter about a ruler’s policies. A “policy → method → result” chart helps learners see the logic of each decision: raids → peace and tax; caliphate → leadership of the Islamic world; gold coins → international trade; new positions → weaker nobility and one nation.
priorKnowledge: The words tax, trade and nation.
anticipatedMisconceptions: He declared himself caliph “partly due to” the Abbasids’ loss of influence; it was one cause, not the only one.
The Spaniards were weary of the Arab nobility, not of Islamic rule.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: on the condition that + base verb · partly due to · whose-clause · not only … but also · by + -ing · cleft It was … that
Notice (Activity 1): on the condition that = only if.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose whose / partly / but also, then rewrite with by + -ing, in order to and a cleft.
Likely errors: *who army · *Part due to · *on the condition that they paid (less formal; accepted but note the text form).
Use (Activity 4): bringing people together.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: abd al-rah-MAN the THIRD, FAT-i-mids, BYZ-an-tines, has-DÂY b. şap-RUT.
Stress: pres-TIGE /preˈstiːʒ/, ar-is-TOC-ra-cy, MER-ce-nar-ies, EN-voys.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can a ruler do to make a country strong at home and respected abroad?”
duringReading: First reading: list his decisions in order.
Second reading: complete the policy → method → result chart.
Find who the Spaniards were weary of.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–13 First reading; 13–20 Policy chart; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: bringing people together; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the Christian states make peace with him?
Why did foreign powers send envoys to his court?
How did he weaken the Arab nobility?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Caliph in 929” and “Gold Coins” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: raids, on the condition that, annual, declared, issued, envoys, promoted.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the policy chart with the methods already written.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short evaluation: “Abd al-Rahman III’s most important decision was … because …”.

formativeAssessment: Explains two decisions and their results.
Explains the policy towards the nobility.
Uses whose and on the condition that correctly.
expectedResponses: The Christian states made peace on the condition that they pay an annual tax. Partly due to the Abbasids’ loss of influence, he declared himself caliph in 929. By giving positions to Christian slaves and Berbers, he weakened the Arab nobility and united all groups into one nation.
content.transferTask: Describe a leader who brought different people together.
content.teacherReflection: Did the chart help learners connect each decision with its result?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “on the condition that” and one with “whose” about this chapter.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the policy towards the nobility.
Uses whose and on the condition that.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: The Small Sultanates
objectives: Explain how the political unity of Al-Andalus disintegrated after 1031.
Analyze why seeking Christian help weakened the Muslims.
Explain the importance of the loss of Toledo in 1085.
Use It was only with … that, lead to + -ing and the past perfect with up to that point.
content.pedagogy: A cause-and-effect chapter. A flow chart (collapse → fragmentation → seeking help → loss of Toledo → realization) shows a chain of decisions with unexpected results. The cleft sentence “It was only with … that …” marks the turning point.
priorKnowledge: Past perfect; cause and result linkers.
The words border, independence and crusade.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The small sultanates did not want the Reconquista; their search for help gave the Christians an opportunity.
Toledo was the second-largest city, after Córdoba.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It was only with … that (cleft) · lead to + object + -ing · past perfect with up to that point / by the mid-11th century · seek assistance
Notice (Activity 1): the cleft marks the turning point.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then shift the focus with a cleft and new subjects.
Likely errors: *led to the Muslims lose · *the heaviest blow they struck up to that point (missing past perfect).
Use (Activity 4): united or divided?
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: re-con-QUIS-ta /ˌreɪkɒnˈkiːstə/, cas-TILE, tu-ley-TU-la, FER-di-nand.
Stress: dis-IN-te-grat-ed, frag-MENT-ed, as-SIS-tance, cru-SADE.
beforeReading: Ask: “What happens to a team when every player plays only for himself or herself?”
duringReading: First reading: who controlled which areas after 1031?
Second reading: complete the flow chart of causes and results.
Find the sentence that marks the turning point.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Team hook; 5–13 First reading; 13–20 Flow chart; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: united or divided?; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the sultanates seek help from the Christian kingdoms?
Why was the loss of Toledo such a heavy blow?
What does “the character of a crusade” mean for the Reconquista?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Small Emirates” and “Toledo, 1085” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: collapse, dynasty, fragmented into, disintegrated, seek assistance, blow, struck against, taken on.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the flow chart with the first and last boxes filled.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph: “How the small sultanates weakened Al-Andalus”, with led to and It was only … that.

formativeAssessment: Uses a cleft and led to + -ing.
expectedResponses: After 1031 Al-Andalus fragmented into small emirates whose primary goal was to defend their own borders. They even sought help from the Christian kingdoms, which led to the Muslims gradually losing power. It was only with the loss of Toledo in 1085 that they realized the danger of the Reconquista.
content.transferTask: Explain what a group can learn from division and unity.
content.teacherReflection: Did the flow chart show the chain of unexpected results?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “It was only with … that …” and one with “led to + -ing”.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains the chain of causes and results.
Uses a cleft and led to + -ing.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Christian Advances and the Fall of Granada
objectives: Trace the Christian advances from 1230 to 1492 on a time line.
Explain why Granada survived longer than other regions.
Describe the life of Muslims in the Christian kingdoms and the start of prejudice.
Use by + past perfect, Of all …, only … and which-clauses.
content.pedagogy: This chapter moves from conquest to the fall of the last stronghold. A time line gives the frame; a two-column chart (their own life / pressure from others) prepares learners for the hard topics of Chapter 8. Discuss prejudice in general terms and calmly.
priorKnowledge: The words crown, marriage and kingdom.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Granada did not defeat the invasion; it survived it until 1492.
The marriage did not make one country at once; it brought the two crowns together.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: by + date + past perfect · Of all …, only … · non-defining which-clause · were forced to · Thus
Notice (Activity 1): Of all the regions, only …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then sort the facts about Muslims in the Christian kingdoms.
Likely errors: *By 1236 he took · *, that brought the two crowns · *forced to dress (missing were).
Use (Activity 4): prejudice and fairness.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: le-ÓN, ar-a-GON, is-a-BEL-la, JAMES the FIRST.
Stress: PEAS-ants, PREJ-u-dice, ac-CEL-er-at-ed, STRONG-hold.
beforeReading: Show the coastal strip of Granada on a map. Ask: “Why might a small region survive longer than larger ones?”
duringReading: First reading: complete the time line (1230, 1236, 1248, 1469, 1492).
Second reading: complete the two-column chart about Muslims after 1248.
Find the word that shows the end: Thus.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Map hook; 5–13 First reading and time line; 13–19 Two-column chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: prejudice and fairness; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does “only Granada comes to mind” when one thinks of Al-Andalus?
What changed for Muslims after 1248?
Why did the marriage of 1469 accelerate events?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Sultanate of Granada” and “Two Crowns” when the picture is in place.
Discuss prejudice in general terms; avoid any comments about groups today.
Word Notes: strip, peasants, districts, prejudice, accelerated, stronghold.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the time line with the years written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph from 1230 to 1492 with by + past perfect and Thus.

formativeAssessment: Places the events on the time line.
Describes the situation of Muslims after 1248.
expectedResponses: By 1236 Ferdinand III had taken control of Córdoba. Of all the regions, only the Sultanate of Granada survived. After 1248 many Muslims lived in the Christian kingdoms as distinct communities, but prejudice began to appear. In 1492 the last stronghold fell.
content.transferTask: Explain how a community can respond to prejudice fairly.
content.teacherReflection: Was the discussion of prejudice calm, general and respectful?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “By … had …” and one with “Of all …, only …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the life of Muslims after 1248.
Uses by + past perfect and Of all …, only.

content.chapter: Chapter 8: The Inquisition and Christianization
content.timing: 45 minutes (or 2 × 40 minutes for this long chapter)
objectives: Describe the policy of compulsory Christianization after 1492.
Explain why the Inquisition was established in 1499.
Analyze how the bans targeted language, names, food, clothing and social habits.
Use such … that, It was decided that and the formal subjunctive.
content.pedagogy: The hardest chapter of the book. Keep the focus on what the text reports and on the idea of identity. Categorising the bans helps learners understand the aim of the policy without retelling every detail emotionally. Do not role-play any of the events.
priorKnowledge: The words religion, identity and law.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The text describes a government and church policy of that time; it is not about Christians or Spanish people today.
Persuasion achieved some success; the Inquisition came because it was found too slow.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: such + noun + that · It was decided that … · demand that + base form (subjunctive) · be subjected to · initially / subsequently / thereafter
Notice (Activity 1): such … that.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the formal passives, then categorize the bans.
Likely errors: *so intense pressure that · *It decided that · *demanded that the baths are demolished (less formal).
Use (Activity 4): identity and respect.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: in-qui-SI-tion /ˌɪŋkwɪˈzɪʃən/, cat-a-LO-ni-a, vi-EN-na.
Stress: com-PUL-so-ry, sub-SE-quent-ly, IM-ple-ment-ed, su-per-VI-sion, de-MOL-ish.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes you feel part of your community?” Collect ideas: language, names, food, clothes, celebrations.
duringReading: First reading: find the choice and the reason for the Inquisition.
Second reading: list the bans and sort them into categories.
Find what happened after 1526.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Identity hook; 5–14 First reading; 14–21 Categorising the bans; 21–25 Quick Challenge; 25–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: identity and respect; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does “one religion” and “one nation” mean as a policy?
Why were the public baths a target?
What does “officially Christian” suggest about the people after 1526?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Granada, 1499” and “The Public Baths” when the picture is in place.
Read this chapter calmly. Allow questions and keep the answers within what the book says.

Word Notes: compulsory, exiled, Subsequently, separate quarters, intense, adopted, accomplish, initially, circles, issue orders, implemented, slaughtered, in accordance with, prohibited, ensured, supervision, properly, demolish, subjected to, provinces, besieged.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the category chart with the headings and one example in each.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short analytical paragraph: “How the bans targeted identity”, using such … that and It was decided that.

formativeAssessment: Describes the choice and the Inquisition correctly.
expectedResponses: After 1492 the Muslims of Granada were given the choice of baptism or exile. Persuasion achieved some success, but church circles found it too slow and established the Inquisition in 1499. The bans targeted language, names, books, food, clothing and the public baths.
content.transferTask: Explain what makes up a community’s identity and why it deserves respect.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners stay with the text and keep the discussion respectful and calm?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “such … that” and one with “It was decided that”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the choice and the Inquisition.
Uses such … that and formal passives.

content.chapter: Chapter 9: Ottoman Support and the Final Expulsions
objectives: Explain the requests for help to the Ottomans and their responses in 1487, 1502 and 1609–1614.
Evaluate the limits on Ottoman help and the efforts made despite them.
Explain the result of Ahmed I’s diplomacy.
Use to which, was unable to … because, Nevertheless and As a result.
content.pedagogy: The chapter balances limits and efforts. A three-row chart (date / limit / response) shows the pattern, and the linkers Nevertheless and As a result carry the argument. It gives a hopeful ending to a sad period: many Andalusians reached Ottoman lands.
priorKnowledge: The names Ottoman, Bayezid II, Kemal Reis.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Bayezid II did not send a fleet in 1487; he wrote letters. The fleet came in 1502.
Ahmed I could not send a navy, but his envoys helped many Andalusians reach safety.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: formal relative clause with preposition (to which) · was unable to … because · occupied with · Nevertheless · As a result · ask someone not to + verb
Notice (Activity 1): a force to which they could look.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose with / Nevertheless / As a result, then correct three verb patterns.
Likely errors: *asked them not oppress · *wished seeking · *unable sending.
Use (Activity 4): help within limits.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: BA-ye-zid the SEC-ond, JEM, MAM-luks, ke-MAL re-IS, AH-med the FIRST, a-bu ab-DUL-lah.
Stress: per-se-CU-tion, op-PRES-sion, ex-PELLED, REF-uge.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can a state help people in another country if it cannot send an army?”
duringReading: First reading: complete the chart (date / limit / response).
Find the poem and what it expressed.
Second reading: What was the final result?
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–14 First reading and chart; 14–20 Limits and efforts discussion; 20–24 Quick Challenge; 24–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–43 Use: help within limits; 43–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the conquest of Constantinople give hope to Granada?
What limited Bayezid II and Ahmed I?
What did the envoy of 1502 present to the sultan?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Poem for the Sultan” and “Kemal Reis” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: occupied with, oppress, achieved, persecution, oppression, rescued, expelled, take action against, seek refuge.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the dates and the limits already written.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write an evaluation: “Was the Ottoman help effective?” with Nevertheless and As a result.

formativeAssessment: Matches the dates with the responses.
Uses Nevertheless and was unable to … because.
expectedResponses: In 1487 Bayezid II was unable to send aid because he was occupied with Cem and the Mamluks, so he wrote letters. In 1502 he sent a fleet under Kemal Reis. Ahmed I could not take action against Spain; nevertheless, he sent envoys, and as a result many Andalusians reached Ottoman lands.
content.transferTask: Evaluate help that was limited by circumstances.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see both the limits and the efforts?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “was unable to … because” and one with “Nevertheless”.

rubricLevels.secure: Matches each date with a response.
Explains the limits and the result.

Build (Activities 2–3): choose the academic phrases, then rewrite with The number of … / The majority of … .

Use (Activity 4): describe a community with figures.

Names: BER-bers, i-BE-ri-an.
Stress: CON-cept, na-tion-AL-ism, AN-ces-tors, em-BRACED.

content.chapter: Chapter 11: Christians, Jews, and Convivencia
content.timing: 45 minutes (or 2 × 40 minutes with the group task)

Use inversion after nowhere, the right to, with certain restrictions and regardless of.
content.pedagogy: A key chapter for intercultural understanding. The jigsaw shares the long reading; the definition task asks for evidence and an honest limit (“with certain restrictions”), so learners avoid both exaggeration and general praise.
priorKnowledge: The words rights, tax and community.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Christians and Jews had rights “with certain restrictions”; the text does not say they had exactly the same rights.

Likely errors: *nowhere else there was · *the right of preserve · *regardless their background.
Use (Activity 4): coexistence today.

Names: con-vi-VEN-ci-a /ˌkɒnvɪˈvenθiə/, JIZ-ya, hrots-VI-tha of GAN-ders-heim.

content.transferTask: Explain what makes coexistence possible today.

content.chapter: Chapter 12: Economic Life

content.chapter: Chapter 14: Andalusian Influence on the West
objectives: Explain how Andalusian knowledge reached medieval Europe (Crusades, translation centers, universities).
Describe the change in European medicine brought by translations.
Describe the influence of Al-Andalus on European architecture.
Use in order to, the first to, contrary to, although and virtually.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains influence. A before/after chart for Europe (before: Dark Ages, demon theory of disease; after: Aristotle, Ibn Rushd in Paris, modern treatment) shows the change clearly. The final paragraph models balanced evaluation (Although few examples have survived …).
priorKnowledge: The words translation, university and architecture.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Crusades did not aim to bring knowledge; they gave Christians the opportunity to become familiar with Islamic civilization.

content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in order to + verb · the first to + verb · contrary to · Until …, there was a belief that … · Although + clause · virtually · not only … but also
Notice (Activity 1): until … / thanks to … began to …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite with although, virtually and but also.

Use (Activity 4): influence across cultures.

Names: SI-ci-ly, ibn RUSHD, PAR-is.
Stress: so-PHIS-ti-cat-ed, in-tel-LEC-tu-al, VIR-tu-al-ly, REP-li-cas, e-VAP-o-rat-ing.

Find the translation centers and the translators.
Second reading: two influences on architecture.

anticipatedMisconceptions: The Alhambra’s name refers to the color of the clay, not to red paint.

Use served as, has been published, quantity + of which and far behind.

metadata.title: Al-Andalus B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Al-Andalus: Spain under Islamic Rule (711–1492)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 17 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow long, dense historical texts with dates, causes, sources and evaluations, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations and balanced arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the history of Al-Andalus: its conquest, golden age, society, economy, science and legacy, and its end, with attention to how the text reports facts, estimates and views.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. Chapters with many names and dates use time lines, charts and maps so that learners organize facts before they discuss them. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (It is known that / It is said that / it can be said that) and attributes views to historians, and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 17 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: time line, cause chain, contrast, thesis and evidence, or attributed view.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world. Long chapters can be divided into two 40-minute lessons.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritise them and the linking words that carry the chapter’s causes, results and contrasts.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context, a map or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus production, exit tickets and the cumulative review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practise it in context. B2 targets include inversion, cleft sentences, formal relative clauses, participle clauses, hedging and reporting. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow extended narration for gist, causes, attributed views and key details.

valuesFocus: D14 Respect — Respect for people of different faiths and backgrounds who lived together.

languageFocus: Every one of the 17 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for evaluation, counterpoints and evidence from more than one chapter, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details, legends or opinions.

Chapters 8 and 9 (the Inquisition, forced conversion and exile) are hard to read. Discuss them calmly and factually. The text describes a policy of that time; it is not about Christians or Spanish people today.
Discuss wars, conquests and defeats factually and without sensationalism; never role-play violence.
Treat all faiths with respect. Convivencia is supported with evidence from the text, not with general praise.
Bracketed Turkish names in the text belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Al-Andalus links a medieval history with questions every community faces: how people of different faiths can live together, how knowledge travels between cultures, and how a community’s identity can be respected.

themes.title: Living together:
themes.description: Muslims, Christians and Jews interacted in Al-Andalus, with certain restrictions (Chapter 11). Discuss what helps diverse communities live together today.

themes.title: Knowledge without borders:
themes.description: Knowledge flowed from Baghdad and Cairo through Al-Andalus to Europe, and translators of three faiths worked together (Chapters 13–14). Compare this with how scientists share knowledge today.

themes.title: Identity and respect:
themes.description: Chapter 8 shows how language, names, food, clothing and social habits make up an identity. Discuss how we can respect the identity of people around us.

themes.title: Help from far away:
themes.description: Chapter 9 shows how people tried to help others in another country. Connect this with how communities help people affected by disasters or conflict today.

actions: Learn and use a greeting in a language spoken by a classmate or neighbor.
Make a short poster about one scientist from Al-Andalus and one thing we still use today.
Find one local charity and write two sentences about what it does.

miniProject.title: A Museum of Al-Andalus
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one room: society, economy, science, architecture or learning. Write a museum label of five sentences with two facts, one exact quotation from the book and one sentence on why it matters today. Use at least two Language Focus patterns such as “is described as”, “thanks to” or “not only … but also”.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Bridge between Cultures
reflectivePrompt.desc: The Arabized Christians, proficient in Arabic and Latin, served as a bridge for cultural exchange (Chapter 11). Write eight to ten sentences about a person or group that connects different communities today. What do they do, and what happens as a result?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect

items.label: D1 Justice

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: The writer separates what is known from what is said or estimated (Chapters 2, 10 and 12).

test.title: End-of-Level Test B2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 85 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.

metadata.title: Al-Andalus B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the history of Al-Andalus alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow dates, causes, sources and evaluations across eight centuries.
Separate facts, estimates and views, and explain the legacy of Al-Andalus with evidence.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 17.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One fact about Al-Andalus that surprised me:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 17 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, justice, helpfulness and honesty with sources. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Christians and Jews participated in social, political and economic life in Al-Andalus (Chapter 11).
Justice: Justice: The agreements protected the religion and property of Christians, while later bans took away the identity of Muslims (Chapters 8 and 11).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Bayezid II and Ahmed I helped the Muslims of Al-Andalus in the ways that were possible (Chapter 9).
Honesty: Honesty: The writer separates what is known from what is said or estimated (Chapters 2, 10 and 12).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 17, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell the story of Al-Andalus in five sentences to someone at home, in your home language or in English.
